segments.title: Fast-firing guns against torpedo boats
segments.summary: The Royal Navy treated E-boat defence as the familiar torpedo-boat problem and answered it with fast-firing guns.
segments.body: The Royal Navy's response begins with a basic tactical question: how do you stop torpedo boats before they complete an attack? The short answer is fast-firing guns. The same principle applies to attacks by small boats more generally, including modern cases. Defenders need weapons that can put effective fire onto a small, fast-moving target during a brief engagement. Gunfire, rather than a matching torpedo attack, is the foundation for the countermeasures discussed in the rest of the video.

evidence.note: The summary identifies fast-firing guns as the answer to torpedo boats and small-boat attacks.

segments.title: Reaction speed against E-boat ambushes
segments.summary: Crowded waters, darkness, small targets, and deception against early radar made reaction speed central to E-boat defence.
segments.body: Engaging a threat at long range is preferable when detection permits it. E-boats were intended to behave as ambush predators and deny defenders that warning distance. Their small size, use of crowded shipping lanes, and night operations could conceal their approach. Attackers could also try to spoof early radar sets and preserve surprise. Defence therefore depended on reacting quickly and bringing enough immediate firepower to drive the boat away or destroy it before the attack developed.

evidence.note: The transcript explains how limited visibility, crowded lanes, and early-radar spoofing demand rapid defensive reaction.

segments.title: Coastal gunboats built to stop E-boats
segments.summary: Steam Gun Boats, Fairmile Ds, and heavily armed small escorts supplied the speed and rapid fire needed for close E-boat engagements.
segments.body: The Royal Navy answered the E-boat threat with numerous small, gun-armed craft that could react quickly and bring substantial firepower to the encounter. These were different from gunboats in the older Insect-class sense, although Insect-class vessels had some success against E-boats in one or two encounters. The main examples here are Steam Gun Boats and Fairmile D craft. They needed the speed to deploy quickly and enough firepower to drive onto an attacker. Small escorts could therefore carry more guns than their apparent role might suggest. Some weapons described as anti-aircraft guns also supplied the rapid fire needed against E-boats once they came within range.

evidence.note: The transcript names Steam Gun Boats and Fairmile Ds, and explains that rapid-firing weapons on small escorts could be intended for E-boat defence.
